posts.title: Talent Pool Software: How to Rank Your Own Database Before You Pay a Job Portal
posts.metaTitle: Talent Pool Software: Rank Your Own Database First
posts.description: We audited 3 million candidate records at one staffing firm: 10% duplicates, 10% junk, 80% still relevant. Portal spend fell from $100 a role to $60.
posts.dek: We audited 3 million candidate records sitting in one firm's Google Drive folders. A tenth were duplicates, a tenth were junk, and 80% were unique profiles nobody had touched in years.
posts.cardImageAlt: Sortinghat evaluation panel: a candidate scored 96, split into weighted criteria with a percentage and written justification for each

faq.q: What is talent pool software?
faq.a: Talent pool software consolidates, refreshes and ranks the candidates a staffing firm has already sourced, so recruiters can search their own database before paying to source externally. It differs from an ATS record store in that the pool is actively kept current and scored against live roles, rather than passively archived.

faq.q: How much of an old staffing database is still usable?
faq.a: In our audit of 3 million candidate records at one firm, about 10% were duplicates and about 10% held no usable company information. The remaining 80% were unique, real profiles that were out of date rather than worthless. Your own split will differ, and a sample audit of 500 records is the only reliable way to know it.

faq.q: Does database-first sourcing replace job portals like Naukri?
faq.a: No. It reduces how often you need them. Genuinely new skill requirements, new geographies and roles you have never worked still justify a fresh portal pull. The change is that these become the exception rather than the default on every role. In our customer data, job portal spend fell from roughly $100 per role to $60.

faq.q: How is candidate scoring different from keyword matching?
faq.a: Keyword matching checks whether terms appear in a CV. Scoring weighs the whole profile against the role's criteria and shows the reasoning behind each part of the result, so a recruiter can verify it rather than trust it blindly.

faq.q: What should you do with duplicate candidate records?
faq.a: Merge rather than delete, and only with a tool that preserves notes, call history, attachments and submission history from every source record. A merge that loses the 2023 note explaining why a client rejected someone will cost you that client's trust when you submit them again.

faq.q: How long can a staffing firm keep candidate data?
faq.a: Retention has to be defensible rather than indefinite. India's DPDP Act and the GDPR both require a lawful basis for holding personal data and a stated retention position. Records with no reachable contact, no placement history and no recent activity are usually a compliance exposure rather than an asset.

posts.title: Hiring Scorecards: How to Turn a Job Description Into Weighted Evaluation Criteria
posts.metaTitle: Hiring Scorecards: Turn a JD Into Weighted Criteria
posts.description: A real hiring scorecard built from one job description, with the eight criteria and their actual weights, and why one candidate scores differently at two firms.
posts.dek: A job description tells candidates about the role. A hiring scorecard tells your team who to reject, and why. Here is one built from a real job description, with the actual weights.
posts.cardImageAlt: Sortinghat job description review: a parsed Director of Engineering role beside structured fields for client, salary and location

toc.label: Why a JD is not a scorecard
How to build your first one

faq.q: What is a hiring scorecard?
faq.a: A structured definition of who qualifies for a role, made up of evaluation criteria, a scoring guideline for each, and a weight reflecting how much each one matters. Candidates are rated against every criterion and the final score is the weighted average, which lets a team evaluate consistently rather than relying on each recruiter's reading of a job description.

faq.q: How is a hiring scorecard different from a job description?
faq.a: A job description is written for candidates and describes the role attractively enough that someone applies. A scorecard is written for the hiring team and defines the decision rule, including what disqualifies someone. One is a sales document, the other is criteria.

faq.q: How do you weight hiring criteria?
faq.a: By asking what the role actually risks failing on, not by what sounds most impressive. On a site-lead hire, team building and operational skills should outweigh specialist technical knowledge, because building the team is the job. Weights of 1 to 5 across six to ten criteria is a workable range.

faq.q: Can the same candidate score differently for the same role at two companies?
faq.a: They should. Same job title does not mean same job. If the criteria and weights reflect what each company actually needs, including company stage and size, the same profile will score differently against each, and that difference is the useful part.

faq.q: How long does it take to build a hiring scorecard?
faq.a: The criteria generate from the job description in one step. The part worth spending time on is adjusting the weights and adding the rules the client believes but did not write down, which is usually a fifteen to thirty minute conversation.

faq.q: How do you test a hiring scorecard before using it?
faq.a: Score two people whose outcome you already know: one you would definitely hire and one you clearly rejected. If the scorecard cannot separate them, it is not measuring the job yet. Adjusting it against three known CVs is far cheaper than discovering the problem after three weeks of submissions.

posts.title: AI Screening Calls: What Gets Asked, Verified and Written to the Record
posts.metaTitle: AI Screening Calls: What They Verify and Capture
posts.description: 70% of candidates complete an AI screening call in 3 to 7 minutes. What it verifies, which CV claims collapse under it, and what reaches the record.
posts.dek: Roughly 70% of candidates complete an AI screening call, and it takes three to seven minutes. Here is what the call is for, which CV claims collapse under it, and what lands on the record afterwards.
posts.cardImageAlt: Sortinghat activity timeline: an automatically logged call written to the candidate record with the stage move attached

faq.q: What is an AI screening call?
faq.a: A structured, automated phone conversation that qualifies a candidate against a specific role: confirming interest, availability, compensation expectation, and the CV claims that matter most for that role. It typically runs three to seven minutes and writes its findings onto the candidate record as structured data rather than as an audio file.

faq.q: Do candidates complete AI screening calls?
faq.a: In our data, around 70% do, with a typical call lasting three to seven minutes. Completion is a real quality metric rather than a vanity one: a call people abandon is selecting for patience, and the candidates most likely to hang up are the ones with the most options.

faq.q: Do candidates have to be told they are speaking to an AI?
faq.a: Yes, in a growing number of jurisdictions. The EU AI Act classifies recruitment AI as high-risk with obligations that took effect on 2 August 2026, and several US states including Illinois have their own disclosure rules for automated hiring tools. Beyond compliance, undisclosed automated calls damage candidate trust for very little gain.

faq.q: Can an AI screening call reject a candidate?
faq.a: It should not. Under the EU AI Act, human oversight of automated decisions is required for high-risk systems, which includes recruitment. Good practice and current regulation point the same way: the AI ranks and flags, a person decides.

faq.q: Is candidate data from AI screening calls used to train models?
faq.a: Not in our case. Call data is stored encrypted, belongs to the client whose candidate it is, and is neither used for model training nor shared with third parties. There is no pooled dataset across customers. Ask any vendor this question directly and expect a one-sentence answer.

faq.q: Which CV claims most often fail verification on a screening call?
faq.a: Quantified impact claims. Percentage improvements, and revenue or GMV figures presented as moving from one number to another. When the call asks a second question about the baseline, the time period or the individual contribution, candidates who did the work answer immediately and those who did not become vague.

posts.title: Natural Language Candidate Search: Five Real Queries, and Why Vague Ones Fail
posts.metaTitle: Natural Language Candidate Search: 5 Real Queries
posts.description: Five real natural language searches run on a live staffing database, what they returned, and the one reason most candidate search queries disappoint.
posts.dek: Real searches run against a live staffing database, the results they returned, and the single reason most natural language queries disappoint the person typing them.
posts.cardImageAlt: Sortinghat search: a natural language query for engineers in Bangalore returning 71 ranked candidates

toc.label: Your own database, not the web
How to test on your own data

faq.q: What is natural language candidate search?
faq.a: Search that takes a plain-language description of the person you want and returns ranked matches, without Boolean operators or manually built filters. It interprets meaning rather than matching keywords, which lets it handle conditions like company stage or institution tier that never appear as literal terms on a CV.

faq.q: Is natural language search better than Boolean search for recruiting?
faq.a: For compound queries and conditions that are judgements rather than keywords, yes. For exact-match requirements such as a specific certification number or a named employer, a filter remains more precise. Most real recruiting searches are the first kind.

faq.q: Why is my natural language candidate search returning poor results?
faq.a: Almost always because the query describes a category rather than a person. A query like 'backend engineer in Bangalore with four years of experience' has three conditions and thousands of matches. Add the specific stack, the institution tier and the domain context, and the result set changes completely.

faq.q: Does natural language search cover LinkedIn and job boards?
faq.a: In our case it searches your own database only. External sourcing is a separate motion with a separate licence cost, and the sensible order is to exhaust what you already own before paying to search elsewhere.

faq.q: Do recruiters still need to learn Boolean search?
faq.a: It remains useful on platforms that only support it, so it has not disappeared. It is no longer a sensible criterion for hiring a sourcer, because describing a profile precisely is now the scarce skill and it is far quicker to teach.

faq.q: How do you write a good candidate search query?
faq.a: Include four elements every time: the capability in detail, the level as a range, the hard constraints such as location and institution, and the context you would actually reject someone over, such as industry or company stage. Queries missing two of these are the ones that disappoint.

faq.a: It runs inside your browser on profiles you open yourself, reads the publicly visible sections of the page you are already viewing, and lets you save that person into your own database against a job or a company. It works at the pace you browse, because it is reading your session rather than running its own automated collection.

faq.q: What candidate data does a LinkedIn sourcing extension collect?
faq.a: Publicly visible profile information: work experience, education, skills and the About section. It does not collect private fields, connection graphs, message content, or anything behind a paid tier you do not hold.

faq.q: Do candidates need to be told their profile is in a recruiter's database?
faq.a: Under the GDPR, the UK regime and India's DPDP Act, notice obligations apply to personal data you hold, including data gathered without direct contact. Our platform can run notice campaigns over email, WhatsApp or call, but they are not enabled by default. Firms placing into the EU or UK should enable them and take their own legal advice on wording and timing.

faq.q: How long is sourced candidate data retained?
faq.a: For as long as the client remains on the platform, after which it is removed. Data is isolated per client, is not pooled across customers, is not used for model training, and is not shared with third parties.

faq.q: Is sourced candidate data used to train AI models?
faq.a: No. There is no cross-customer training set and no secondary use of client data. This is a question worth asking every vendor you evaluate, and worth being suspicious of any answer that takes more than a sentence.

faq.q: Is scraping LinkedIn profiles legal for recruiters?
faq.a: The position depends on jurisdiction, on the platform's own terms, and on how the data is collected, stored and used. What matters legally is the basis on which you process personal data rather than the label attached to the method. Ask any vendor to state, in writing, what they collect, where the collection happens, and on what basis.

posts.title: Staffing KPIs: The Four Numbers a Firm Owner Should Check Every Day
posts.metaTitle: Staffing KPIs: The 4 Numbers to Check Every Day
posts.description: Fill rate and time-to-fill are lagging indicators. The 4 staffing KPIs that move first, how to read each one when it falls, and the 10-minute daily routine.
posts.dek: Fill rate and time-to-fill are outcomes. By the time they move, the decision that caused them is six weeks old. Four numbers move earlier, and together they predict next month's revenue closely enough to act on.
posts.cardImageAlt: Staffing pipeline with candidates across stage columns, each showing a match score of 96, 93 or 92

toc.label: Why fill rate is the wrong daily number
What to do when one moves
Where four numbers is not enough

faq.q: What KPIs should a staffing agency track daily?
faq.a: Live submissions, interviews scheduled, offers in play, and receivables past 60 days. These are leading indicators that can still be influenced. Fill rate, time-to-fill and gross margin are lagging and belong in weekly or monthly reviews rather than a daily check.

faq.q: What is the difference between leading and lagging recruitment metrics?
faq.a: Leading metrics predict future outcomes and can still be changed by acting today. Lagging metrics report results that are already determined. Most recruitment dashboards are built almost entirely from lagging metrics, which is why they feel informative but rarely change anyone's behaviour.

faq.q: Why is time-to-fill a poor daily metric?
faq.a: It is measured from a start point you often do not control to an end point the client controls. A slow client can double it while your team does everything right. Checked daily it produces anxiety rather than decisions, and it moves on noise.

faq.q: How do you forecast staffing revenue from pipeline?
faq.a: Take offers in play, apply your own historical offer-to-join rate, and add stage-weighted values from earlier pipeline. Accuracy depends entirely on using your own conversion rates rather than industry averages, because conversion varies more by firm than by market.

faq.q: What does a falling submission-to-interview ratio mean?
faq.a: That the team is busy and the work is not landing. Pull the last ten rejections and read the reasons. If they cluster around one requirement, the brief was wrong. If they scatter, the screening was. It is the most expensive failure mode in staffing because it burns capacity without producing anything.

faq.q: Why should recruiters see receivables?
faq.a: Because the recruiter holds the relationship that unblocks the payment. Most overdue invoices in staffing are stuck on a query that one conversation resolves, and finance does not have the relationship to make that call.

posts.title: Recruiter Admin Time: Where the Hours Actually Go, and What Automatic Capture Removes
posts.metaTitle: Recruiter Admin Time: Where the Hours Actually Go
posts.description: A candidate's history lives across 5 channels and the record holds one. What recruiter admin costs, and what automatic capture must produce to remove it.
posts.dek: A candidate's history lives across five channels. The record holds whichever one the recruiter remembered to log. Here is what that costs and what automatic capture has to produce to fix it.
posts.cardImageAlt: Candidate record showing experience, location, full career timeline and channel actions for call, WhatsApp, LinkedIn and email

toc.label: Why the record is never current
How to measure your admin load

faq.q: How much time do recruiters spend on admin?
faq.a: Industry reporting consistently puts non-recruiting work at the majority of a recruiter's week, covering data entry, logging calls, updating stages and rebuilding context. The only number that matters for your firm is the one you measure on your own team, which takes one unannounced day of time tracking across three recruiters.

faq.q: What is automated call logging in a recruitment CRM?
faq.a: It captures conversations across phone, email, WhatsApp and LinkedIn and writes them onto the candidate record without anyone typing. The useful version extracts structured fields such as notice period and compensation, rather than only storing a transcript that somebody still has to read.

faq.q: What is the difference between a transcript and structured capture?
faq.a: A transcript is the words that were said. Structured capture pulls the facts out of those words into fields that can be searched, filtered and reported on. Only the second one saves time, because a transcript on a record still requires a human to read it before the record is usable.

faq.q: Does automated call logging require candidate consent?
faq.a: Recording consent rules vary by jurisdiction. India, several US states and the EU all impose requirements, and some require disclosure before recording begins. If your desks place across borders, the requirement is set by the candidate's location rather than your office's.

faq.q: Why is WhatsApp integration important for recruitment in India?
faq.a: In India, WhatsApp is often the primary channel candidates actually reply on. A system that does not thread WhatsApp into the candidate record will always hold an incomplete history, because the most current part of the conversation sits on an individual recruiter's phone.

faq.q: What should a delivery manager be able to see without asking anyone?
faq.a: The true state of every desk: which candidates were contacted, what they said, which submissions are live and where each one is stuck. If that requires a status meeting to establish, the logging is not working and the meeting is compensating for it.

posts.title: Candidate Response Rates by Channel: Call, WhatsApp and Email Compared
posts.metaTitle: Candidate Response Rates: Call vs WhatsApp vs Email
posts.description: Out of 100 candidates contacted for a strong role, about 40 respond to a call, 25 on WhatsApp and 12 to 15 by email. What that means for your sequence.
posts.dek: Out of 100 candidates contacted for a strong role: about 40 respond to a call, 25 on WhatsApp, and 12 to 15 by email. Here is what that means for how you sequence outreach.
posts.cardImageAlt: Candidate record header showing direct call, WhatsApp, LinkedIn and email actions alongside experience and location

toc.label: What the numbers do not tell you

faq.q: What is a good candidate response rate?
faq.a: In our own outreach on well-paid, credible roles, roughly 40 out of 100 people respond to a phone call, 25 respond on WhatsApp and 12 to 15 respond by email. Weaker roles perform materially worse on every channel, so treat these as a ceiling rather than an average.

faq.q: Which channel gets the highest response from candidates?
faq.a: The phone, by a clear margin, followed by WhatsApp and then email. This surprises teams who assume messaging has replaced calling. A call is harder to ignore and easier to answer in thirty seconds, and it carries an implicit signal that the role is worth a person's time.

faq.q: How many times should you follow up with a candidate?
faq.a: Four touches across roughly ten days, changing the channel each time. Beyond that, additional messages damage your brand more than they generate replies, and the person who was going to respond has already done so.

faq.q: Is WhatsApp appropriate for recruitment outreach?
faq.a: In India it is a normal and well-received channel when the message is relevant and clearly identifies you. In other markets it can read as intrusive. Match the channel to the market rather than to your own preference.

faq.q: Should you include salary in the first message?
faq.a: Including a band consistently improves reply quality, because it filters out mismatches before they cost anyone a call. Our channel response rates are measured on roles with strong compensation, and that is not a coincidence.

faq.q: Why is my recruitment outreach getting no replies?
faq.a: Usually the segment, not the copy. A precise segment with average wording outperforms brilliant wording sent to a broad list. If the positive reply rate is low while the raw reply rate is fine, the segment was wrong.

posts.title: High Volume Recruiting: What One Screening Day Actually Produces
posts.metaTitle: High Volume Recruiting: What One Day Produces
posts.description: A recruiter makes 40 calls a day and submits 3 or 4. What changes when 1,200 profiles are filtered to 300 contacts, and where the approach stops working.
posts.dek: A recruiter makes about 40 calls a day and finds 3 or 4 people worth submitting. Here is what changes when the pool is filtered first, and where the approach stops working.
posts.cardImageAlt: Staffing pipeline with candidates across stage columns, each showing a match score of 96, 93 or 92

toc.label: When it is the wrong approach

faq.q: How many calls can a recruiter make in a day?
faq.a: Around 40 on a full calling day, which on a good day converts to 3 or 4 candidates worth submitting. The ceiling is not dialling speed. It is that most of those 40 were never viable, and the recruiter finds that out one conversation at a time.

faq.q: How many candidates can be screened in a day with AI calling?
faq.a: In our own delivery, a filtered shortlist of roughly 300 people is contacted by call, email and WhatsApp in parallel, producing around 10 submission-ready profiles within a few hours. On a high-volume QA role we submitted 120 profiles in a single day, because the pool was deep and the criteria were wide.

faq.q: What roles suit high volume recruiting?
faq.a: Roles with clear, checkable eligibility criteria and a deep candidate pool. Volume QA, support, sales development and entry to mid engineering all work. Senior, confidential and executive searches do not, because the first conversation is a sell rather than a qualification.

faq.q: Does volume screening hurt candidate experience?
faq.a: It depends entirely on relevance and disclosure. A well-targeted call that respects someone's time performs better than a recruiter leaving 300 voicemails. A poorly targeted one at scale is worse than doing nothing, because you have annoyed 300 people instead of 40.

faq.q: How many profiles should you submit per role?
faq.a: Fewer than you can. Volume screening should produce a small evidenced shortlist, not a large list of everyone who passed. The exception is genuine high-volume hiring, where the client is filling many seats and wants breadth.

faq.q: What happens to candidates who do not make the shortlist?
faq.a: They return to the pool with a logged reason and freshly confirmed availability. That segment is the warmest list you own for the next similar role, which is the compounding argument for working your own database first.

posts.title: Recruitment CRM: What It Should Do Beyond Storing Names
posts.metaTitle: Recruitment CRM: What It Should Do Beyond Leads
posts.description: A staffing CRM has 3 jobs: win the client, deliver the role, collect the money. Most do one. What the other two require, from LinkedIn capture to the brief.
posts.dek: A staffing CRM has three jobs: win the client, deliver the role, collect the money. Most tools do the middle one and treat the other two as somebody else's problem.
posts.cardImageAlt: Contact record showing experience and company, with direct call, WhatsApp, LinkedIn and email actions

toc.label: What a CRM will not fix

faq.q: What is a recruitment CRM?
faq.a: A system that manages the client and prospect relationships that generate roles, as distinct from an ATS which manages candidates through a hiring process. Staffing firms need both, and running them as separate systems means the client brief gets retyped and the relationship history gets split.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ATS and a recruitment CRM?
faq.a: An ATS is organised around the requisition and closes the record when the role closes. A CRM is organised around the relationship, which outlives any individual role. The hiring manager who moves companies and the client who goes quiet for a year are both CRM problems that an ATS cannot hold.

faq.q: Can a recruitment CRM add leads from LinkedIn?
faq.a: Ours does, in one click from the profile, including fetching contact details and filing the person against the right company. The alternative is a recruiter copying a name into a spreadsheet, which is where most staffing business development quietly dies.

faq.q: Do staffing firms need a separate sales tool?
faq.a: Most do not, and the separation causes more problems than it solves. A generic sales CRM does not understand requisitions, submissions or placements, so the two systems end up being reconciled by hand every month.

faq.q: How does a CRM help with business development?
faq.a: By replacing a static prospect list with live signals. Researching which roles a company is currently hiring for turns a generic pitch into a specific one, and specificity is most of what separates a reply from a deletion.

faq.q: What is a staffing-specific notetaker?
faq.a: A meeting assistant that understands recruitment context, so a client call produces a structured brief with requirements, constraints and timelines rather than a generic transcript. The value is that the delivery team receives what the client actually said, not what the salesperson remembered.

posts.title: AI Interviews: How the Questions Are Built, What Gets Scored, and Where the Human Sits
posts.metaTitle: AI Interviews: How Questions Are Built and Scored
posts.description: AI interview questions built from 3 inputs: the job description, the weighted criteria and the company. What gets scored, and where the human must sit.
posts.dek: An AI interview is only as good as its questions, and most are drawn from a generic bank. Here is what changes when they come from the role's own criteria instead.
posts.cardImageAlt: Evaluation criteria screen showing generated criteria with descriptions and editable priority weights, plus a field for adding custom criteria

faq.q: How are AI interview questions generated?
faq.a: From three inputs: the job description, the weighted evaluation criteria for that role, and the company context. Each question traces back to something being assessed, which is what separates a role-specific interview from a generic question bank sorted by job title.

faq.q: Can an AI interview reject a candidate?
faq.a: It should not. The EU AI Act classifies recruitment AI as high-risk and requires human oversight of automated decisions. The workflow that holds up is the AI ranking and flagging, with a person making every rejection and every submission decision.

faq.q: Is AI interviewing legal?
faq.a: It is regulated rather than prohibited, and the requirements differ by jurisdiction. The EU AI Act, NYC Local Law 144, Illinois AIVIA and the Colorado AI Act all impose obligations around disclosure, bias auditing and human oversight. The rules follow the candidate's location, not your office's.

faq.q: What should an AI interview actually score?
faq.a: Verifiable facts such as notice period and compensation, evidenced claims about what someone built or owned, and inferred signals such as structure and domain fluency. The third group carries the least confidence and should carry the least weight, which is where most tools go wrong.

faq.q: How is an AI interview different from an AI screening call?
faq.a: A screening call qualifies: interest, availability, compensation and the CV claims that decide the submission. An interview assesses capability against the role's criteria in more depth. The first is about eligibility, the second is about fit.

faq.q: What is a good completion rate for an AI interview?
faq.a: There is no cross-industry standard worth relying on. Measure your own, segment it by role type and seniority, and treat a falling rate as a design problem rather than evidence of candidate quality. Candidates with the most options abandon first.

posts.title: Duplicate Candidate Records: Why They Happen, What They Cost, and How to Prevent Them
posts.metaTitle: Duplicate Candidate Records: Why They Happen and Cost
posts.description: In a 3 million record audit, about 10% were duplicates. How they enter, what email-based matching catches and misses, and what a merge has to preserve.
posts.dek: In a 3 million record audit at one firm, about 10% were duplicates. Here is how they enter, what identifier-based matching catches and misses, and what a merge has to preserve.
posts.cardImageAlt: Candidate record showing experience, current company, location, full career timeline and education on a single consolidated profile

faq.q: Why do duplicate candidate records happen?
faq.a: Four routes, all of them normal operations rather than mistakes: the same person applies to several roles over time, a recruiter uploads a CV without checking, a referral arrives with a different spelling or address, and bulk imports land without matching. Duplicates are a by-product of a working desk, not evidence of a careless one.

faq.q: How do you deduplicate a candidate database?
faq.a: By matching on an identifier at the point of entry rather than cleaning up later. We use email address as the unique key. That catches the common case cleanly, and it will not catch someone who applies from a work address and later a personal one, which is the main gap to plan around.

faq.q: What percentage of a staffing database is duplicated?
faq.a: In our audit of 3 million records at one firm, roughly 10% were duplicates and another 10% held no usable company information. Your own split will differ by firm age and hygiene, and a sample of 500 records is the only reliable way to establish it.

faq.q: How fast does candidate contact data go stale?
faq.a: Job titles and employers decay fastest, followed by work email addresses, then phone numbers. A candidate placed two years ago is very unlikely to hold the role your record states, which makes the record wrong rather than the person irrelevant.

faq.q: Should you delete old candidate records?
faq.a: Records with no reachable contact, no placement history and no recent activity cost more in search noise than they provide in value. Data protection law in most jurisdictions also requires a defensible retention position rather than indefinite storage, so deletion is a compliance step as well as a hygiene one.

faq.q: What should a merge preserve?
faq.a: Everything attached to every source record: notes, call and message history, attachments, submission and placement history, and stage changes with their timestamps.
